reviews.title: Wild Blue Skies Review: Bland Homage
reviews.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for Wild Blue Skies.
evidence_points: Wild Blue Skies is not shy about the video game experience it is trying to emulate. You are Bowie, an anthropomorphic dog in a spaceship making your way through a series of levels, most on rails, some taking place in small open areas, to defeat the evil Grimclaw, an anthropomorphic tiger with a giant cyborg head. Developer Chuhai Labs and Vitei Backroom Inc. are transparently presenting their take on Star Fox 64 – a noble and welcome endeavor – but many shortcomings prevent it from reaching the nostalgic heights of its inspirational arcade action game.

Mechanically, controlling your ship feels okay, but it dips into slog territory more often than I would like. The perspective of the reticle makes it hard to see what you’re firing at (and there is no first-person option), and hitting the occasional wall bounces you around like a pinball. It can be especially frustrating on the open-ended levels that are not on rails. Locking on and firing your standard lasers are also mapped to separate buttons, meaning you have to choose between the two actions, which is limiting. Also, the range to lock on to fire an extra powerful homing shot is too short. By the time I locked on to enemies, it was often too late, and the enemy had disappeared off-screen.

The look of Wild Blue Skies is attractive, though, with bright colors and cool ship designs. I like the look of the main cast and their performances, along with the performances of all the bosses and secondary characters. Everyone’s characterization, however, leaves a lot on the table. The bosses all boast and yell with unfounded confidence, and I felt bad when teammates complained when I accidentally (allegedly) shot them. But even with the quality acting, everyone is undefined and generic. Dialogue could be swapped among the characters, I don’t think I would even notice.

The levels offer some visual variety, but are also generic. Moving from a desert level to an ice level is a nice change of pace, but little has been done to make them feel novel. Also, many of the on-rails levels begin with characters pointing out the limited visibility, whether in a storm or from snow. Narratively, I like flying through a hurricane in a game like this, but when the elements keep making things hard to see, it feels like a story excuse for poor draw distance. When you do make it through the hailstorm, or the tornado, or the lava flows, the bosses at the end arguably take too long to defeat.

Like its Star Fox 64 inspiration, there are incentives to replay the campaign to chase different challenges and see the alternate paths. Seeing the game to credits is completely doable, but I got frustrated by moments of unfair challenge. Health drops are infrequent, and deaths are often the result of running into a stray enemy, bouncing against walls, or getting overwhelmed by screen-filling danger that I didn’t feel equipped to avoid. It made many defeats feel like the game’s fault rather than my own, which is especially annoying when burning through lives sends you back to the beginning of the campaign.

Bowie and pals’ adventure successfully impersonates the Star Fox 64 experience, but it’s an underwhelming impression. Nostalgic moments and satisfying action appear occasionally, but it pays homage to a fault and doesn’t find space to present its own personality. It has the unfortunate timing of releasing and being compared to this year’s Star Fox on Switch 2 – an excellent remake of Star Fox 64. But even if I did not have that game in my immediate memory, I would be hard-pressed to identify anywhere that it has improved on the genre with design lessons learned since 1997, or even risen to meet the ones that already existed even 30 years ago.

reviews.title: PC Review - 'Wild Blue Skies'
reviews.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for Wild Blue Skies.
evidence_points: Some of the appeal of the indie game sector comes from a sense of renewal: taking a beloved game or franchise that hasn't seen a new entry in years and creating a spiritual successor that captures what made the original so well loved. We've seen this with cult hits like Jet Set Radio and in genres like Metroidvanias , with indie developers often stepping in to fill the void left by dormant franchises. Star Fox is a good example. While the original is available on the Switch 2, the lack of a new or remastered entry during the Switch era has led to games like Whisker Squadron: Survival and Fur Squadron . Wild Blue Skies is the latest game to carry that torch, and it's good, even if it hews a little too closely to its source material.

The scientist Grimclaw once worked for the army, but his desire for power ultimately brought the world to war. The military turned to the mercenary group known as the Blue Bombers to fight back, resulting in victory and Grimclaw's retreat to the northern volcanic lands. Years have passed, and Grimclaw has returned with a new fleet of robotic forces under his command. Once again, the Blue Bombers have been called into action, and a new generation of pilots has answered the call.

The similarities extend to the mechanics as well. This is an on-rails shooter where most levels automatically propel you forward from a third-person perspective behind the jet. You can use air brakes or a boost to slow down or speed up while still having some freedom to move your craft around the screen. You can fire your lasers normally or charge them for a more powerful shot, with both being upgradeable through power-up rings. Bombs can also be collected, although they deal damage within a splash radius rather than clearing the screen. Your teammates are present during missions, but while you can occasionally save them from enemy fire, you don't feel their impact on the battlefield very often.

Certain boss fights provide the only major mechanical deviation, allowing you to fly around more freely within a confined area. The game automatically turns you around when you reach the boundaries of the fight. Missions are a decent length, with most containing no more than one checkpoint, while boss fights punctuate every level with opening quips and farewell messages. The levels are straightforward but contain plenty of secrets and branching paths that can lead to high-scoring bonuses. Finding those paths requires performing specific actions that aren't always immediately obvious.

Perhaps the most notable element that none of the other modern Star Fox -inspired games has adopted is the lives system. You have three lives for your entire run, along with a health meter that only partially refills between levels. Losing all three lives means starting over from the first stage, but your high scores remain saved. This gives the game an old-school mentality where you need to improve through repetition rather than brute-force your way to the end. That's especially fitting given that a full run can be relatively short.

The game does make some changes to Nintendo's formula, although they're relatively minor compared with other Star Fox -inspired titles. There is no cockpit view, and you can only fly a spacecraft rather than transforming into a land vehicle. The charged shot is assigned to a different button than the regular laser, while the lasers can be set to rapid-fire mode by holding down the button. This is a welcome change that saves you from potentially suffering from carpal tunnel during a run. You also can't perform somersaults or U-turns during the free-flight sections, but those sections aren't particularly common.

The game's straightforward approach may catch some players off guard. Games inspired by older titles often try to put their own spin on the formula. Whisker Squadron: Survival turned Star Fox into a roguelike, while both Fur Squadron games added leveling and upgrade systems. Even the Switch 2 release of Star Fox adds plenty of cut scenes to freshen up an otherwise familiar experience. Wild Blue Skies does none of that, instead going straight into the action with only brief pauses between missions. That approach works well, making the game feel decidedly old school while helping it stand apart from its contemporaries.

It helps that the core mechanics are absolutely solid. Flying feels great, with a responsive ship that can turn on a dime without requiring you to fight the controls. Shooting feels good as well, but it would've been nice to continue firing the lasers while charging a shot, since those actions use separate buttons now. The levels are well paced, and the difficulty never feels overwhelming. In short, Wild Blue Skies nails nearly everything you'd expect from the Nintendo 64 classic, making it easy to pick up and play. The only notable omission is multiplayer, but the secrets and branching paths provide enough replayability to make that a relatively small loss.

Graphically, the game benefits greatly from its cel-shaded art style. Colors are bright throughout, and everything remains highly readable. The cut scenes and character portraits also look fantastic, with plenty of detail, but more varied expressions would have been nice. The frame rate is solid, with little effort required to maintain 60fps. My only real complaint is the contrails behind your ship. They look cool, but removing them in favor of greater screen readability would've been preferable.

The sound is pretty good overall. The music captures the vibe of the Nintendo 64 classic remarkably well, with each level featuring an action-focused track that doesn't try to be overly cinematic. The sound effects are distinct, and the voice work is solid across the board. There is some repetition in the end-of-level status reports, but it never becomes particularly annoying.
